# The GitHub Actions autonomy loop

How a filed issue becomes a merged pull request with nobody watching, and every mechanism that keeps the chain from going quiet.

```
  merged PR    run ended `blocked`/`paused`   issue closed `done`   manual dispatch
      │                     │                          │                   │
      ▼                     ▼                          ▼                   ▼
auto-assign-next.yml  handle-failure.yml  agentic-chain-on-close.yml  agentic-trigger.yml
      └─────────────────────┴──────────────┬───────────┴───────────────────┘
                                     ▼
                        [agentic-assign] oldest assignable `ready` issue
                                     │  ready → in-progress, then post the assignment comment
                                     ▼
                  "<mention> — autonomous pipeline assignment for issue #N …"
                                     │  the comment IS the trigger
                                     ▼
             claude-runner.yml  ─or─  opencode-runner.yml   (whichever mention matched)
                                     │  orchestrator → pipeline skill → TDD → PR with
                                     │  `Closes #N` + `READY TO MERGE`
                                     │  [agentic-run-state]  settled nothing? one more attempt
                                     │  [agentic-rescue]     still nothing? push what exists,
                                     │                       report it, label the issue `blocked`
                                     │                       (unless the run already settled it)
                                     │                                     │
                                     ▼                                     ▼
                              auto-assign-next.yml              handle-failure.yml
                                     │  merge → close #N,          │  report the failure,
                                     │  label `done`               │  then chain unless the
                                     └─ [agentic-assign] ──────────┴─ cascade brake is tripped
                                              next `ready` issue → back to the top

   the branch off that path: the PR opened, CI reported, and CI was red
            │
            ▼
   agentic-ci-failure.yml  ── on `workflow_run` CI completed + failure
            │  the run that opened the PR is normally still here, waiting on this
            │  very verdict through `[await-ci]` — so the workflow declines while
            │  a run on this PR or its issue is live, and `agentic-watchdog.yml` re-raises it later
            ▼
   "<mention> — CI is red on this pull request …"  → the runner, on the same PR
            │  fix on `pipeline/feature-<N>`, push, CI again
            └─ green → the merge gate → back into the loop above
               limit spent → PR to draft, issue `blocked` → handle-failure.yml
```

## Four ways in, and nothing else

One entry per terminal state, which is the whole design: a run ends in exactly four
states, and each one has a workflow subscribed to the event it raises.

| Entry | Fires on | Covers |
|-------|----------|--------|
| `agentic-trigger.yml` | manual dispatch | A human starting the pipeline on the oldest assignable `ready` issue. This is how a run begins from a standing start |
| `auto-assign-next.yml` | `pull_request: closed` with `merged == true` | Chain from the merge to the next issue. This is how a run begins from the previous one succeeding |
| `handle-failure.yml` | `issues: labeled` with `blocked` or `paused` | Chain past a run that halted without merging, and report what happened. This is how a run begins from the previous one *not finishing* |
| `agentic-chain-on-close.yml` | `issues: closed` on an `agent-task` issue | Chain past a run whose deliverable was never a diff — an answer, an executed command, a set of filed issues — so it closed its own issue `done` and opened no PR. This is how a run begins from the previous one succeeding *without merging anything* |

**Nothing else may start a session on a new issue.** Filing an issue, labelling one `ready`, reopening one, and the passage of time all leave the queue exactly where it was.

There is one path that starts a session without assigning anything, and the distinction is the whole of why it is allowed: `agentic-ci-failure.yml` hands a **pull request that already exists** back to the agent that already owns it. It selects no issue, reads no queue, and changes no label on the happy path — see "A red CI is nobody's report" below. `agentic-intake.yml` still reacts to `issues: opened, reopened`, but only to keep the label definitions present and to drop a stale `done` from a reopened issue — it assigns nothing. `agentic-watchdog.yml` still sweeps hourly, but only to release issues whose runs died; it does not restart the queue itself — the `blocked` label it applies does, through `handle-failure.yml`, which is why that label must be applied with the PAT.

**The third and fourth entries are what make the loop closed.** A halted run is terminal exactly as a merge is, and both outcomes have to release the queue: with only the first two entries, every failure parked the pipeline until a human dispatched the trigger, which on a repository with nobody watching means until somebody noticed. It fires on either halt label, differing only in what it reports — `blocked` asks a human for the clarification the run is missing, `paused` states that the issue is already requeued behind the dependency the run filed and asks for nothing. The chain is bounded rather than unconditional — see the cascade brake below.

**The fourth closed the last hole in it**, and it stayed open far longer because the state it covers looks like success. A run whose deliverable is an answer, a command or a set of filed issues closes its own issue and labels it `done`: no pull request, so `auto-assign-next.yml` never hears anything; no halt label, so `handle-failure.yml` never fires; no `in-progress` left behind, so the watchdog has nothing to sweep. Three of the four terminal states had a subscriber and the fourth had none, and every document in this tree said there were three ways in — so nothing read as broken. On 28 Aug 2026 issue #557 ended `blocked` and chained correctly to #807; #807's run filed twelve follow-up issues, closed itself `done` at 19:41:07, and the pipeline stopped with 23 `ready` issues queued behind it. `agentic-assign` had carried the `closed_without_pr` guard for this case since it was written, and had never had a caller. Same cascade brake as the halt chains: a `done` close is a success but not a *merge*, so it resets nothing and must not restart a queue the brake has parked.

A `ready` issue can still sit in the queue indefinitely, because nothing is scheduled to notice it. Events genuinely do get lost — GitHub keeps one pending run per concurrency group and drops the next, a webhook can be missed — and when that happens the chain stops until a human dispatches `agentic-trigger.yml`. That is the remaining trade: an idle pipeline is preferable to sessions nobody asked for.

## Issue labels are the loop's state machine

| Label | Means | Applied by | Cleared by |
|-------|-------|-----------|-----------|
| `agent-task` | The pipeline owns this issue | The issue form, or an agent authoring the issue | — |
| `ready` | Meets the **Definition of Ready** (`agentic-issue-creation`) and waits in the assignment queue | The issue form, an agent authoring the issue, or a human adding it by hand | `agentic-assign`, on assignment — or `agentic-intake.yml`, the moment the issue does not meet the Definition of Ready, with a comment naming what is missing |
| `in-progress` | A run owns it. The assigner counts this label as a live run, against `AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS` | `agentic-assign` | The merged-PR chain, the run itself when its deliverable is not a diff, `agentic-rescue` when the run ended without finishing, or the watchdog |
| `blocked` | This run ended without finishing; a human has to answer something. The queue does not wait on it — the label is itself an entry point | The run, `agentic-rescue`, or the watchdog | A human, by adding `ready` |
| `paused` | This run ended without finishing, and what it is waiting on is an **issue it filed**, not a person. Applied *alongside* `ready`, with that issue set as this one's `Blocked by`: the queue skips it while the dependency is open and picks it up again once the dependency merges. Also an entry point | The run, or `agentic-rescue` inheriting it | `agentic-assign`, on the next assignment |
| `done` | Meets the **Definition of Done** (`agentic-autonomous-pipeline`): closed as completed, deliverable landed, nothing left in flight | The merged-PR chain, or a run releasing a non-PR deliverable — and the close chain, for such a run that forgot it | `agentic-intake.yml`, on reopen |
| `decision-review` | A default the run chose, revisit at leisure. Carries no `ready`, so it never enters the queue | The run — see `agentic-decision-autonomy` | A human, by adding `ready` |
| `scope:*` | The areas the issue's change stays inside — part of the Definition of Ready, and what the assigner reads to decide what may run side by side | The issue form's Scope field (applied by `agentic-intake.yml`), an agent authoring the issue, or a human | — they stay after the issue closes, as the record of what it touched |

Intake never applies `agent-task` or `ready` itself — that would take label assignment out of the hands of whoever files the issue. `agentic-assign` selects on `ready`, so an issue only becomes *selectable* once something puts `ready` on it: the "Agent Task" form's own `labels:` default, an agent following `agentic-issue-creation`, or a human adding it by hand — including to resume a `blocked` issue, or to opt a free-form/API-filed issue in.

**`ready` is held to the Definition of Ready.** Its machine-checkable part — `agent-task`, and one or more `scope:*` labels, every one known (`readinessVerdict` in `assignability.cjs`) — is enforced twice with one verdict. `agentic-intake.yml` takes `ready` off an issue that fails it, on open and whenever `ready`, a scope or `agent-task` arrives or leaves, and comments what is missing; `agentic-assign` refuses the same issue, so one that slipped past intake still never reaches a session. Intake does apply scope labels in one case: an issue filed through the "Agent Task" form, whose required Scope field is the filer's own declaration. Nothing is read out of free text. Every write intake makes uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so none of it raises an event.

`ready` marks an issue as **eligible**, never as **started**. The label puts it in the queue; only one of the four entries above takes it out again. This is the distinction to hold on to when reading anything below that talks about an issue "entering the queue": entering the queue is not being picked up.

**An issue is released by whoever finishes it.** A run whose deliverable is a pull request is released by the merge. A run whose deliverable is an answer or an executed command releases its own issue — closes it, labels it `done`, drops `in-progress`. Skipping that leaves the run holding its slot — and, at the default of one slot, the whole queue — after it already succeeded, until the watchdog ages it out and reports it as lost.

## Two rules keep the loop alive

1. **Comments must be posted with `PAT_TOKEN_COPILOT_AUTOMATION`.** A comment created with `GITHUB_TOKEN` triggers no workflow, so the loop stops silently. The same applies to the PR: one opened with `GITHUB_TOKEN` raises no `pull_request` event, leaving `auto-assign-next.yml` dormant. The inverse is also load-bearing: the `label` job's own housekeeping (ensuring the label definitions exist, dropping a stale `done` on reopen) runs under `GITHUB_TOKEN` precisely so it raises no event the workflow could retrigger on — intake itself never applies `ready`, so this only matters for the labels it does still touch. The rule reaches `git push`, where it has to be enforced differently: `git push` reads no token from the environment, so a step that merely sets `GH_TOKEN` pushes with whatever credential the job's git configuration holds — and after the agent step that is the agent's own GitHub App token, which no `permissions:` block can grant `workflows` to, because there is no such key. A branch differing from `main` on a workflow file is then rejected outright. `agentic-rescue` pushes to an explicitly authenticated URL so the PAT is the credential actually used.

   **The agent step needs the PAT stated twice.** `claude-code-action` exports its own `github_token` input into the session environment, overriding the step-level `GH_TOKEN` — so that input is the identity `gh pr create` actually runs under. Left as `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the PR is authored by `github-actions[bot]`, and GitHub creates its `pull_request` workflow runs already parked as `action_required`: "N workflows awaiting approval", no CI, no `auto-assign-next.yml`. Both `claude-code-action` steps in `claude-runner.yml` therefore pass `PAT_TOKEN_COPILOT_AUTOMATION` as `github_token`. `opencode-runner.yml` needs no equivalent — opencode reads `GH_TOKEN` from the step environment and overrides nothing.

   **A consequence to respect:** under the PAT, everything the session posts is authored by a real user rather than a bot, and the runners' trigger guard filters on `comment.user.type != 'Bot'`. An agent-authored comment containing the agent's own mention would therefore wake a new run. **No comment written by an agent session may contain `@claude` or `@opencode`.** Exactly two comments in the whole system carry a mention, and both are written by a workflow rather than by a session: the assignment comment from `agentic-assign`, and the CI handback from `agentic-ci-failure.yml`. Each is a deliberate trigger, each is bounded, and each must be posted with the PAT for the same reason — under `GITHUB_TOKEN` the author is a bot and the runners filter it out, so the trigger would be written and never read.
2. **The assignment comment carries the whole assignment.** It names the issue, mandates orchestrator-first delegation, states the branch names, the verification expectation, and the PR conventions. Its text is identical for every agent apart from the mention on the first line — the runtimes read the same instructions.

An issue the agent closes without opening a PR raises no `pull_request` event, so the merge chain cannot carry it. The runners used to carry their own step for that case; it was removed, and correctly — a run starting the next run is the pipeline deciding to run again on its own. What was missing was the other half: with the runner's step gone and nothing put in its place, the state had no subscriber at all and the queue went idle every time a run delivered something other than a diff. `agentic-chain-on-close.yml` is that half. The runner still assigns nothing; it releases its issue — closes it, labels it `done`, drops `in-progress` — and the close is the event a workflow reacts to, with the queue and the cascade brake in view, which is exactly what a runner does not have.

## How many runs at once

At most `AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS` issues hold `in-progress` at a time — default 1, which is single flight exactly as the pipeline ran before the variable existed. Four mechanisms keep several live sessions from colliding, and each covers a different failure:

| Mechanism | Where | Prevents |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| **Capacity** | `selectNextAssignable` in `assignability.cjs` | More sessions than configured. An issue keeps `in-progress` until its run is finished — merged, halted or closed — so the label is the count of live runs, and every entry point fills every free slot it finds |
| **Scope** | `scopeClaim` in `assignability.cjs` | Frequent collisions. Above 1, an issue starts beside the live runs only when its `scope:*` labels clash with none of theirs |
| **Entity exclusion** | Both runners' `run-name` and concurrency group | Two sessions on one issue or one pull request — two branches for one issue, two pushes to one branch |
| **The merge gate** | `agentic-auto-merge.yml` — "The merge gate" below | Two pull requests that are green alone and red together reaching `main`. This is the one that makes parallel runs safe; the other three make them efficient |

**Scope is a throughput hint, never a safety property.** Over 384 merged pipeline PRs, two adjacent ones shared a file 36% of the time; pairs whose `src/` scopes were disjoint still did 7% of the time — the locale files, `balance.ts`, `main.ts`, `GameState.ts`, the mirrored skills. No label keeps those apart, and none needs to: the gate refuses to merge a head that does not contain `main`'s tip and hands a conflict back to an agent. What a scope buys is that the gate rarely has to.

**Scope labels.** `scope:engine`, `scope:nav`, `scope:economy`, `scope:world`, `scope:ui`, `scope:renderer`, `scope:console`, `scope:scenarios`, `scope:pipeline`, `scope:global` — the one taxonomy is `SCOPES` in `assignability.cjs`, `agentic-intake.yml` keeps the labels defined from it, and `agentic-issue-creation` says which to pick. An issue may carry several, and must carry one to meet the Definition of Ready. Two scopes run alone whatever else the issue declares:

- `scope:global` — the change spans many areas at once, and says so;
- `scope:pipeline` — a change to the agentic layer (workflows, actions, decision modules, agents, hooks, `agentic-*` skills) rewrites the rules every live run is following, and landing it with nothing else in flight means no run straddles the old rules and the new. A `gameplay-*` or `dev-*` skill takes the scope of the code it documents.

A *live* run can carry no scope, or one nobody knows, having been assigned before scopes existed. It fails closed the same way: it claims the whole repository, and nothing starts beside it.

**An older issue holds its place.** An issue that could run but for a scope clash holds its claim for the rest of the pass, so nothing younger that overlaps it starts first; an older unlabelled issue holds everything, and the queue drains until it can run alone. No clock is involved — the hold lasts exactly as long as the clash. Only an issue that is otherwise assignable holds a place: one waiting on a dependency does not, or a paused issue would hold the very scope its own blocker needs.

**What is counted.** A pull request waiting on the gate still holds its issue's slot and scope until it merges, which is right: a same-scope run must not start on a `main` that lacks the pending change. A human mentioning an agent by hand starts a session outside the count, exactly as a human dispatching the trigger is outside the queue; its entity group still keeps it off any other session's issue or pull request. A CI or conflict handback on a pipeline PR is not counted either — its issue already holds the slot.

Two guards keep the count honest:

- **`agentic-assign` defers.** When the live runs fill the limit — or one of them runs alone — the action logs why and assigns nothing; finishing a run re-enters the step. It defers whether or not those issues have a linked PR, and **it never diagnoses**: a run 40 seconds old and a run that died hours ago look identical from the labels alone, so declaring one lost belongs to the watchdog, which is the only mechanism that ages it. `agentic-assign` used to comment "Pipeline halted — no linked PR was created" on sight, which it posted on #404 while that run was one minute into a two-hour session.
- **The entries share a concurrency group.** A merge and a `blocked` label can land in the same second, and each would read the live runs before either wrote `in-progress`. Every assigning job therefore declares `concurrency: agentic-assignment`, repo-wide, `cancel-in-progress: false`, and that group is the one place `in-progress` is added. Only the assigning job: `auto-assign-next.yml` splits waking the merge gate into a separate job precisely so it stays *out* of the group, since GitHub keeps one pending run per group and drops the rest.

**Each runner run names what it works on.** Both runners set `run-name` to `agentic-run issue-<N>`, `agentic-run pr-<N>` or `agentic-run manual`, and a trigger the job will skip to `agentic-noop`. That name is the only identity a run carries in `listWorkflowRuns`, and every liveness check reads it (`run-liveness.cjs`): "is a session live on this issue" is no longer "is any runner run live", because with several sessions there always is one. A run whose name carries no identity — a run from before `run-name` existed, a manual dispatch naming no issue — counts as working on anything, the direction that never declares a live session lost. The concurrency group is keyed by the same entity, `agentic-runner-<entity>`, shared by name between `claude-runner.yml` and `opencode-runner.yml`, `cancel-in-progress: false`. It is not the cap — GitHub has no "at most N" primitive, and capacity is `agentic-assign`'s — it is what keeps two sessions off one issue or one pull request.

  Both workflows trigger on every `issue_comment`/`pull_request_review_comment` in the repository, with no content filter at that level — only the job's own `if:` decides whether the comment was a real mention. Before #572/#610, *every* such run still claimed the shared group on its way to resolving `if:` false, so a burst of irrelevant comments (a session's own trailing wrap-up comment among them) could drop a real, already-queued assignment before its job ever started. The `group:` expression mirrors the job's `if:`: only a trigger that will actually act joins an entity's group, everything else gets an isolated group keyed by its own run id. Per-entity groups make the eviction rarer still — it now needs two pending runs for the same issue or pull request — and `autonomy-loop.test.ts` evaluates both expressions against real event payloads.

  A drop can still happen in principle — two genuine mentions on one entity racing, a webhook truly lost — so it is not written off as impossible. `agentic-recover-blocked` is the last step of every session: if some *other* issue is `in-progress` with no PR and no queued or live run of its own, that assignment was dropped, not merely slow, and this labels it `blocked` immediately — same predicate the watchdog uses, without waiting for its hourly sweep. `agentic-trigger.yml` remains the manual fallback.

  A run genuinely queued is not always reported `queued` — the Actions API can report it `pending`, `waiting`, or `requested` depending on exactly what it is blocked on. #614 is what checking only `queued`/`in_progress` costs: a real, correctly-queued run came back `pending`, the narrower check missed it, and the issue was labelled `blocked` 21 seconds into a session that went on to open its PR. Every liveness check now reads runner runs through `runnerRuns` in `issue-api.cjs`, which polls the full non-terminal set — `queued`, `in_progress`, `waiting`, `requested`, `pending` — and unions it with an unfiltered listing, so neither a seconds-old run (#1136) nor an hours-old one buried under noop runs is missed.

## Halt conditions

The loop stops while the `in-progress` issues fill `AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS` — or one of them runs alone — when no assignable `ready` issue remains or fits beside the live runs, and when the cascade brake trips. Neither halt label stops it: the issue either names is finished, and `handle-failure.yml` chains to the next assignable issue while reporting what happened on the one that stopped. Its comment states what happened to the queue — moved on to #N, idle, or parked — because that is the part a human cannot infer from the issue alone.

Resuming a **blocked** issue is a human act: add `ready` to put it back in the queue — the issue must meet the Definition of Ready, or intake takes the label back off and says why. The label alone starts nothing, and if a rescued draft PR is still open against the issue it will not be selected at all until that PR is closed or merged.

Resuming a **paused** issue is not. That is the whole difference between the two: the run that paused already put `ready` back on, already recorded the dependency it filed as this issue's `Blocked by`, and already left its partial work on a draft PR labelled `paused`. `assignability.cjs` skips the issue while the dependency is open — and, uniquely, does *not* skip it for that open PR, because a `paused` PR is a handover rather than a run in flight. When the dependency's PR merges, the issue is assignable again and the next assignment tells the run to continue on the handover branch. Nobody has to remember it, and nobody should close the handover PR to "clean up": closing it discards the work, merging it lands a half-finished change.

**The handover is the PR on the issue's own `pipeline/feature-<N>[-<runId>]` branch, and nothing else.** A `paused` PR that merely writes `Closes #N` is not one — its branch belongs to whichever issue's run opened it. #730's did, on 25 Aug 2026: its handover PR #740 also carried `Closes #758` for a defect the same run had fixed in passing, so #758's assignment was answered with #730's handover and told, in the assignment's own words, that "a previous run on this issue" had left work on `pipeline/feature-730-32642264036`. That run finished on #730's branch, took `paused` off #740 and marked it ready — and #730, its carve-out gone, was skipped by every assignment afterwards with "pull request #740 is already open against it" while the queue took another issue and nothing reported it. `resumeTargetFor` now reads only the `pipeline` entry `deliverableFor` head-matches, and `assessCandidate` exempts that one PR rather than any paused one.

A run that dies without labelling anything — OOM, a hung tool call, the job timeout, a revoked token, a turn ended on outstanding work — would otherwise leave its issue `in-progress` forever and halt the chain silently. `agentic-watchdog.yml` sweeps hourly: an issue `in-progress` past `AGENTIC_STALL_MINUTES` with no linked PR is commented on, labelled `blocked`, and stripped of `in-progress`. That labelling is what surfaces the failure, so the watchdog must use the PAT — a label applied with `GITHUB_TOKEN` raises no `issues: labeled` event and `handle-failure.yml` would never fire.

One cause never needs that hour: a run whose own triggered job was cancelled while still queued behind another session, per "How many runs at once" above. Nothing about that failure is a crash to wait out — the session that was occupying the slot is right there, finishing normally, and its own last step (`agentic-recover-blocked`) is the one already positioned to notice and label it `blocked` on the spot. The watchdog remains the floor underneath it: the case where nothing is left alive to notice at all.

The linked-PR skip in that sweep has a blind spot of its own, and the watchdog carries a second sweep for it: an open, non-draft `pipeline/feature-<N>` PR with a failing channel on its head — any workflow's, not `ci.yml`'s alone — is handed to `agentic-ci-failure.yml` by dispatch. It decides nothing itself — every guard stays in the fail-safe — so this is the same event raised again, not a second opinion about it. See "A red CI is nobody's report".

**Only a step that can see the run end may declare it lost.** That is a rule about evidence, not about seniority. `agentic-assign` sees labels alone, where a run 40 seconds old and one that died hours ago are indistinguishable, so it defers and never diagnoses. The watchdog ages the run against a threshold, which is inference — correct, but hours late. The runners' own post-agent steps have the one thing neither has: they run *after* the session is over, in the same job, so "this run finished and produced nothing" is an observation. They are allowed to settle the issue for that reason, and the watchdog remains the floor for the runs that never got that far — a job killed before its post-steps, a dropped webhook.

## The run is retried before it is written off

A session can end early for reasons no instruction reaches: a backgrounded delegation whose notification never arrives, a crash in the first minutes, a transient API error, a model that simply stops. Every one of those wastes a whole assignment and, before the retry existed, a whole day — #404 waited four hours for a watchdog sweep, and #406 sat `in-progress` after dying in 58 seconds.

`agentic-run-state` answers one question after the agent step: is the issue in a terminal state? Terminal means a linked pull request, a `blocked` label, a `paused` label, or a closed issue. Anything else means the session stopped with the work unfinished, and the runner starts one more attempt in the same job — carrying what went wrong, an inventory of the `pipeline/*-<N>` branches the previous attempt left on disk (never pushed, so visible nowhere else), and the rule that most often broke it. The retry is gated on the clock as well: with less than `min_remaining_minutes` of the job budget left, the run is written off rather than cut off mid-work, because a cancelled job takes its unpushed branches with it.

One retry, not three. A real run takes over two hours, so a second attempt is all a 360-minute budget holds — and the failures worth retrying die early and leave the whole budget behind.

The job's `timeout-minutes` is the outer bound only. Each agent step carries its own, smaller one — 270 minutes for the first attempt, 80 for the retry — so an attempt that overruns *fails its step inside a live job* instead of cancelling the job: the state check, the retry and the rescue all run with clock left. Runs 565, 591, 606 and 609 (#921, #947, #953, #956) ended on the job clock with neither, because a cancelled job skips the retry gate and gives the rescue seconds. The retry step runs under `always()` for the same reason: a step without it is skipped after any failed step, so on the verdict alone the gate could only ever fire on an attempt that exited 0 having done nothing.

## Rescue: a run that ends early must not end silently

Intent is not a mechanism, so `agentic-rescue` runs last in both runners, with `if: always()` — it also covers the crash, the job timeout and the cancelled run, none of which the agent can write instructions for. It pushes the branch this run built — `pipeline/feature-<N>-<runId>`, or whichever branch of that family is on disk — if commits exist on it and opens a **draft** PR carrying `Closes #<N>` and no `READY TO MERGE`; when no feature branch was produced, or the branch is empty, it comments on the issue saying so. A push it cannot complete is reported too, with the rejection, the commit list and the diffstat of what is being lost: a step that ends on `::error::` alone leaves exactly the silence this action exists to prevent, since the job log is not somewhere anyone is watching. Either way the failure becomes visible immediately and the work survives, instead of surfacing hours later as a watchdog sweep over an issue whose branches no longer exist.

**Every outcome here labels the issue `blocked` — unless the run already settled it**, because reaching this step at all means the run did not finish it, and by then the session is over, so there is nothing left to wait for. That includes the successful rescue: an issue left `in-progress` with a draft PR attached passes both the single-flight check *and* the watchdog's linked-PR skip, so it would hold the queue for as long as the draft stayed open. `blocked` is the honest state — work preserved, human notified by `handle-failure.yml`, queue released.

The exemption is checked before anything is *said*, not only before the label is applied. An issue that is closed, `blocked` or `paused` was settled by the run itself, which has already explained itself on the thread; commenting again contradicts it, and re-labelling a `paused` issue would be worse than duplicate — `blocked` would take it back out of the queue the pause had just returned it to, stranding it and its handover branch until somebody noticed. Issue #707 is the case: its run reported an unrunnable channel, filed the defect behind it, and escalated exactly as the skill asks, and the rescue step still commented that it had "concluded that no code change was needed without saying so", one comment under where it said so.

One detail follows from the exemption. A run that paused itself and then died before opening its own handover PR would otherwise be rescued into a trap: the issue is back at `ready` waiting for its dependency, and an unlabelled draft PR would make it unassignable to everyone forever. So a rescued branch on a `paused` issue inherits the `paused` label, and the handover works anyway.

The rescue PR is a diagnosis, not a deliverable: unreviewed and unvalidated by definition. Finishing it or dropping it is a human decision — and it has to be made *before* `ready` goes back on the issue, because an issue with an open PR against it is not assignable. That is not an obstacle to work around; it is what stops a second run being told to build a branch that already has commits on it.

**No runner chains to the next issue itself.** A run starting the next run is the pipeline deciding to run again on its own, and a runner has no view of the queue it would be restarting. The chain belongs to a workflow reacting to the event the run's own ending raised: `handle-failure.yml` on the `blocked` or `paused` label, whoever applied it — the run, `agentic-rescue`, or the watchdog — and `agentic-chain-on-close.yml` on the close of an issue the run settled itself. Both weigh the chain against every other halt since the last merge; neither is reachable from inside a session.

## The cascade brake

Chaining from a halt is what keeps an unattended queue moving, and it is also the one mechanism that can run away with itself. A systemic failure — an expired token, a broken `main`, a runner image that no longer builds — fails every run identically, and an unconditional chain would march through the entire backlog halting each issue in minutes. That risk is why the chain did not exist before.

`agentic-assign`'s `after_blocked_run` and `after_paused_run` guards bound it. Before chaining, either counts the runs that have halted under **either** label **since the pipeline last merged one of its own pull requests**, and stops at `AGENTIC_BLOCKED_CHAIN_LIMIT` (default 3). Both labels count, and counting only one would leave the brake open to the other: a pause is the healthier outcome, but a broken `main` produces a queue full of pauses just as readily as it produces blocks. An issue wearing both labels counts once, and the handover pull request `listForRepo` returns alongside issues counts for nothing — the run that opened it already counted through its own issue. A merged pipeline PR is proof the loop can still finish something, so it is what resets the count; nothing else does, and no clock is involved. When the brake trips the guard posts one notice — marked with an HTML comment so a second trip does not stack another — naming the count, the limit, and the two ways out: fix what the runs have in common and dispatch the trigger, or merge any pipeline PR.

**With several runs live, a systemic failure halts them in a wave.** The brake trips on the halt that reaches the limit; runs already live when it trips can still halt after it, each chaining into a parked queue and assigning nothing. So the worst case is `AGENTIC_BLOCKED_CHAIN_LIMIT + AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS − 1` halts before the queue is parked, and every one of them is reported on its own issue.

Two smaller guards sit in front of the count, and both are about not chaining from something that was never a run. The issue must still carry the label the guard fired on, and it must have carried `in-progress` at some point — a human labelling a backlog issue `blocked` is filing a note, not ending a session. The guard also drops a leftover `in-progress`, since either halt means the run is over and the labels cannot both stand: left on, it would defer this very assignment against a session that no longer exists.

## What may be assigned

The rules live in `.github/scripts/assignability.cjs`, required from the workspace by `agentic-assign` rather than written inline in the action, so every entry point decides identically and the decision is unit tested against the source that ships (`tests/unit/config/assignability.test.ts`). **Every rule fails closed.** A fact the module cannot establish — an issue it cannot read, a dependency graph larger than it will walk — blocks, and an idle queue is recoverable in a way a run started on absent ground is not.

An issue is skipped when:

| Condition | Why |
|-----------|-----|
| It carries `blocked`, `in-progress`, or `done` | Respectively: halted, already owned, already finished. `done` on an open `ready` issue is contradictory, not a permission |
| It does not meet the Definition of Ready | No `agent-task`, no `scope:*` label, or a scope nobody knows. Without a scope the assigner cannot tell what the issue may run beside. Intake takes `ready` off such an issue as well; this is the half that holds when intake never ran |
| It is a pull request | `listForRepo` returns PRs alongside issues; one carrying `ready` would be assigned as a task |
| An **open** pull request carries it | A deliverable PR — one from its own `pipeline/feature-<N>` branch, or one GitHub records as closing it — is open, so the branch has commits a second run would collide with or silently duplicate. This is the state a rescued issue is left in. A PR that merely *mentions* the issue is not this: #567's own body cites half the backlog, and under a mention predicate that one PR froze it |
| A declared dependency is still open | The ordinary case, and the transitive one — the whole declared graph is walked, not just the first level, because a human can close an issue by hand while the issue *it* declared is still open |
| Its `blocked_by` relationships **could not be read** | A failed call is not an empty list. Only the feature being absent (404/410) falls back to the body section |
| A declared dependency was closed as **not planned** | Closed is not delivered. The work was abandoned; whatever declared it is still missing its ground |
| A declared dependency is closed but an **open PR** still carries it | The headline case. The issue is closed, the code has not merged, and `main` does not have it — issue #547 with PR #566. Both deliverable arms are checked: the dep's own pipeline branch, and its closing references |
| A declared dependency **is** a pull request that has not merged | A `Blocked by` line may name the PR rather than the issue it closes |
| A declared dependency **cannot be read** | A typo in a `Blocked by` line used to read as "no dependency" and start the run anyway. Unverifiable counts as unmet |
| Its pull requests **could not be read**, by any path | A failed deliverable read is `unknown`, and unknown blocks — a 500 must never read as "no pull request". Every read is retried on a transient status first, and the closing-PR read falls back to REST before giving up (below), so this now means *nothing* answered rather than *one thing* answered badly. A pass that ends with nothing assigned and any candidate unread **fails the step** — see below |
| Its dependency graph exceeds 40 issues | A malformed body, and an unwalked graph is an unverified one |

### Where a dependency comes from

Two sources, unioned, and an issue stays blocked until every member of the union has landed.

**GitHub's own `blocked_by` relationships are the authority** — the Relationships panel on an issue, read through `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}/dependencies/blocked_by`. A relationship is a *declaration*: nothing about quoting an issue in prose can produce one, which is exactly what a body reference cannot promise. `agentic-issue-creation` sets them; the endpoint takes `issue_id`, the database id rather than the issue number, which is the detail that fails silently when guessed.

**The body section is the secondary source**, kept because every issue written before relationships existed carries its dependencies there and nowhere else. Dropping it the moment relationships arrived would make that entire backlog instantly assignable — a regression in the property the relationships are being adopted for. It is read strictly, because a mention is not a declaration: a section opens on a heading (`## Blocked by`), a bold line (`**Blocked by**`), or a line *starting* with the phrase (`Depends on: #12`), and ends at the next heading or bold line. A phrase inside a sentence opens nothing, so `## Context` citing #55 as background declares nothing — and neither does a bullet reading "depends on the rework in #123".

A relationship call that fails for any reason other than the feature being absent is `unknown`, and `unknown` blocks. A 403 or a 500 must never read as "this issue has no dependencies"; a repository without the feature at all is a different fact, and there the body section is simply the only source there is.

### What counts as an issue's pull request

Everywhere the loop asks "does this issue have its PR" — the parallel-run count, the watchdog's leave-alone, the run-state settle check, and the two assignability rules above — the answer is the **deliverable predicate**: a PR whose head is in the issue's own branch family — `pipeline/feature-<N>` or `pipeline/feature-<N>-<runId>`, since every run names its branches after itself — (open or merged; closed-unmerged is a rejected deliverable), or a PR GitHub records as closing the issue (`closedByPullRequestsReferences`, open and merged only). A timeline cross-reference counts for nothing: any PR that merely writes `#N` in prose raises one, which is how docs PR #561's passing mention of #547 read as run #133's deliverable and disarmed its retry with five hours of budget left. The predicate is inlined in `agentic-watchdog.yml` and `agentic-run-state` because both run without a checkout, and shared from `issue-api.cjs` for everything `agentic-assign` decides; all copies are pinned identical in shape by `autonomy-loop.test.ts`.

**One degraded API surface must not park the queue.** The two arms are read independently, each retried on a transient status (408, 429, 5xx, or a network fault) before it counts as failed. When `closedByPullRequestsReferences` stays unavailable, the closers arm falls back to the REST timeline: a cross-referenced PR whose *body carries a closing keyword* for the issue, open or merged only. The keyword is what keeps the fallback from being the mention predicate #568 removed — a PR that only cites the issue writes none. It is narrower than the field it replaces, since a PR linked by hand in the sidebar carries no keyword either; that is the accepted cost. On 17 Aug 2026 that field answered 503 for every candidate, three dispatches of `agentic-trigger.yml` in a row skipped the entire `ready` queue, and issue #554 sat unassigned behind three green runs.

**A queue that was not read is not an idle queue.** A refusal carries which of the two it is, and `agentic-assign` fails the step when a pass assigns nothing while any candidate went unread — naming each one. The step is otherwise indistinguishable from an empty backlog, and a green Actions row is all a human dispatching the trigger ever sees of it.

**Undeclared coupling is not detected, and deliberately so.** Comparing an issue's `## Files` list against the files an open pipeline PR touches was considered and rejected: on this repository nearly every gameplay issue touches `GameState.ts` or `GameLoop.ts`, so a single stale draft PR would make the whole backlog unassignable — the exact stall the blocked-chain exists to prevent. Measured again for parallel runs, 36% of adjacent pipeline PRs share a file, most of them in files that merge cleanly. An issue that depends on another's work says so in its `Blocked by` section; that is what `agentic-issue-creation` is for. Coupling nobody declared is what the merge gate catches: a PR merges only on a head that already contains every earlier merge, with CI green on the result.

## Repository variables

| Variable | Values | Effect |
|----------|--------|--------|
| `AGENTIC_AGENT` | `@claude` / `@opencode` (leading `@` and case optional; unset means `@opencode`) | The agent that assignment comments address, and therefore the runner workflow that starts |
| `AGENTIC_AUTO_ASSIGN_ENABLED` | `true` / anything else | Whether a merged pipeline PR chains to the next ready issue. Set to anything else, the manual trigger is the only way a run ever starts |
| `AGENTIC_AUTO_MERGE_ENABLED` | `true` / anything else | Whether the merge gate runs at all. Off, nothing merges a `READY TO MERGE` PR and every issue with one holds its slot until a human merges it |
| `AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS` | positive integer, default `1`; anything else falls back to `1` rather than opening the gate | How many issues may hold `in-progress` at once. Above 1, issues run side by side only when their `scope:*` labels are disjoint; `scope:global` and `scope:pipeline` run alone. Every entry point fills every free slot. "How many runs at once" holds the rules |
| `AGENTIC_STALL_MINUTES` | minutes, default `420`; a value below the runners' 360-minute job timeout is clamped up to it | How long an issue may stay `in-progress` without a linked PR before the watchdog marks it `blocked`. Below the job timeout it would sweep live runs |
| `AGENTIC_LOOP_BUDGET_MINUTES` | minutes after the job started, default `180`; anything else falls back to the default rather than opening the budget | When the session's loop deadline falls — exported as `AGENTIC_LOOP_DEADLINE_EPOCH`, read by the orchestrator before every delegation. Past it no pipeline loop starts a new iteration; the linear steps still run. The loop budget section of `agentic-autonomous-pipeline` holds the rule |
| `AGENTIC_BLOCKED_CHAIN_LIMIT` | positive integer, default `3`; anything else falls back to the default rather than disabling the brake | How many runs may end `blocked` since the last merged pipeline PR before the chain from a failure parks the queue |
| `AGENTIC_CI_FIX_ENABLED` | anything but `false`, default on | Whether a red CI on a pipeline PR is handed back to the agent. Off, a red CI reports to nobody again — the state PR #581 was left in |
| `AGENTIC_CI_FIX_ATTEMPT_LIMIT` | positive integer, default `3`; anything else falls back to the default rather than disabling the brake | How many times the same pull request may be handed back for a red CI before it is parked as a draft with its issue `blocked` |
| `AGENTIC_RUN_LIVENESS_GRACE_MINUTES` | minutes, default `5`; anything else falls back to the default | How long `run-liveness.cjs` gives a just-assigned run to become visible in `listWorkflowRuns` before its absence counts as evidence the run is lost, rather than merely not-yet-visible |

Switching agents is a one-value change: set `AGENTIC_AGENT` to `@claude` and every subsequent assignment comment mentions `@claude`, waking `claude-runner.yml` instead of `opencode-runner.yml`. Both runners stay enabled either way, so a human can still summon the other runtime by commenting its mention by hand. An unrecognised value fails the assignment step loudly rather than silently picking a default.

## The merge gate

The orchestrator includes `READY TO MERGE` in the PR body when PR status is `ready`; draft versus ready logic is `agentic-pipeline-pr-management`. `agentic-auto-merge.yml` is the one workflow that merges a pull request, and its action is the one place the merge endpoint is called.

**The rule: green on top of `main`.** A marked PR merges only when every channel on its head is green *and that head already contains its base branch's tip*. So the tree that lands on `main` is a tree CI has passed. Green alone was the rule while only one session ran and `main` moved only through that session's own merge. With several sessions live, two pull requests can each be green and be red together — a rename and a new caller of the old name, a threshold and the scenario that pinned it — and merging both would put a `main` on the branch that no channel ever ran. The gate, one PR at a time, in order:

| The head is | The gate | Why |
|-------------|----------|-----|
| `dirty` — conflicts with the base | Hands it to `agentic-ci-failure.yml` | Only an agent resolves a conflict. Decided first: nothing else about the head matters until the base merges into it |
| Red on any channel | Hands it to `agentic-ci-failure.yml` | The fail-safe owns a red PR, and re-checks every guard itself |
| Still running, or reporting nothing at all | Waits | CI completing is the event that brings the gate back. A head with no runs is never green |
| Green, but behind its base | Merges the base into it (`update-branch`, `expected_head_sha` pinned) | CI runs again on the result. `mergeable_state` cannot say this: with no required checks GitHub reports `clean` for a branch that is behind |
| Green on a head containing the base's tip, every required job actually run | Merges it (`squash`, `sha` pinned) | The one state that merges |

**The lock.** The gate runs under a job-level `agentic-merge` concurrency group, `cancel-in-progress: false`, so no two sweeps can each find a different PR up to date with the same `main` and merge both. Job-level because a workflow-level group is claimed before the job's `if:` resolves, and a skipped run would evict a pending sweep that was going to merge — #572/#610's eviction, in another group. GitHub keeps one pending run per group and drops the rest, which is harmless only because **every sweep evaluates every open pull request**, oldest first: whichever sweep survives reads them all. After a merge, the same sweep finds every other green PR behind and brings it up to date. With `k` PRs green at once, the last re-runs CI up to `k − 1` times — bounded by `AGENTIC_MAX_PARALLEL_RUNS`, and the price of never merging an untested combination.

**When it looks.** Never on a clock. Every wake is an event that can change a verdict:

| Wake | Why |
|------|-----|
| `workflow_run`: CI completed with `success`, any branch | On a PR head, that PR may merge now — PR #499 was verified, marked and green, and sat open for want of this trigger. On `main`, every open PR may now be behind |
| `workflow_run`: `Claude Pipeline` or `OpenCode Pipeline` completed, `run-name` starting `agentic-run ` | That session's PR may be marked and green already, and a conflict the fail-safe declined to hand back while the session was live can be handed back now. The noop run every comment creates wakes nothing |
| `workflow_dispatch` from `auto-assign-next.yml` | A marked or pipeline PR's own events — the marker arriving in an edit, a draft marked ready — after CI already finished, when no CI event is coming |
| `workflow_dispatch` from `agentic-watchdog.yml` | Hourly while any marked PR is open: a webhook that never arrived, a sweep that failed on a transient read |

**The marker decides, never the account.** A PR authored by `github-actions[bot]` raises `pull_request` workflow runs that GitHub creates and immediately parks as `action_required`: no CI, no `auto-assign-next.yml`. PR #430 sat open that way, fully verified and marked, with zero checks, holding its issue and the queue behind it. The runners pass the PAT as the agent step's `github_token` so every pipeline PR is authored by a real user and its runs start unprompted — but the gate still releases parked runs on every marked PR it reads, because a PR opened by hand with `GITHUB_TOKEN` still lands parked, and selection here must never branch on who opened a PR. The release needs `actions: write` on the PAT.

**Nothing else merges, and native auto-merge is never switched on.** Before the gate, three places could merge a pipeline PR — the runner that opened it, `auto-assign-next.yml` on the PR's own events, and the CI-completion sweep — each on one PR's head alone, which is exactly the merge that lands two separately-green PRs onto an untested `main`. The runners no longer carry an arming step, and `auto-assign-next.yml` only dispatches the gate. GitHub native auto-merge would merge whenever GitHub's own requirements hold; on this repository, with no required checks, it was always refused (`Pull request is in unstable status`) and every merge already happened inside the action — but switched on anywhere it would be a merge the gate never judged. PR #434 is the other reason it is gone: the `enablePullRequestAutoMerge` mutation named its variable `$method`, which @octokit/graphql rejects before the request leaves the runner, and both arming paths threw on every call and reported success.

**Every refusal is decided on the PR's state, never on the wording of the error.** A refused update or merge is read back: a head that moved is its own new CI run's business, `dirty` goes back to the agent, and anything else — a protection rule, a missing token scope — is `stuck`.

**What fails the step.** A marked PR that can neither merge, update, wait nor be handed back is `stuck`, and so is one whose run-level success hides a required job that never ran (#615). A non-draft PR from `pipeline/feature-<N>` with no marker fails the step too: PRs #507 and #508 were opened that way, each promising `READY TO MERGE` "once the CI jobs report", and with no step anywhere coming back to write it they held their issues indefinitely — the pipeline's own branch means the pipeline's own PR, and that PR ships marked or says why it does not. Each of these holds its issue and its parallel-run slot, and a warning in a job log is not somewhere anyone is watching. Waiting, updated and handed-back PRs do not fail it: each is a state something is already coming back for.

## A red CI is nobody's report

Every path above ends at a merge or at `blocked`. There was a third ending nothing owned: **the pull request opened, marked, and its CI came back red.**

`agentic-auto-merge.yml` declines to run at all when the CI run that woke it concluded `failure` — correct on its own terms, since a failed run has nothing to merge and sweeping it would restate a red check as a red workflow. But declining is not reporting. No merge fires, so `auto-assign-next.yml` never chains. The watchdog leaves the issue alone precisely because a pull request *is* linked to it. And the session that could have read the verdict exited minutes before it arrived. PR #581 sat there — green on every channel its own session ran, two interaction-mode shards red in CI — holding issue #552 `in-progress` with the whole queue behind it, until a human noticed.

Two mechanisms close it, at different distances, and neither replaces the other:

| Mechanism | Owns | Reaches |
|-----------|------|---------|
| `[await-ci]`, the last step of `agentic-pipeline-finalization` | The run reads its own verdict, in the turn that opened the PR. `npm run ci:await` listens to the workflow runs on the head, with no deadline of its own; RED is work, GREEN ends the run | Every run that is still alive when CI reports — which is the normal case, because the wait is what keeps it alive |
| `agentic-ci-failure.yml`, on `workflow_run` CI completed + `failure` | Posting the failure back to the agent as a fresh task on the same PR, with the failing jobs and their log URLs named | The crashed session, the job timeout, the run that pushed a fix and ran out of budget, the CI run that reported an hour later |
| The merge gate's handback step, on any marked PR that is red or conflicts with its base | Dispatching the fail-safe for a PR the gate cannot merge and the agent must fix. The gate reads every run on the head, so this reaches a red check no trigger enumerates | The red that is not CI's — PR #773's `closing-keyword-guard`, with `ci.yml` itself green and no `workflow_run` failure event to fire on — and a conflict with `main`, which has no event of its own at all |

The fail-safe is guarded so it cannot fight the step:

- **Only the issue's own branch family** — `pipeline/feature-<N>` and `pipeline/feature-<N>-<runId>`. CI failing on `main`, on a human's branch or on a harness branch summons nobody. The suffix is not optional: since #554 every branch a run creates carries its run id, and this pattern was anchored without it, so it matched **no branch any run actually pushes**. The whole fail-safe was dead code from that day until PR #773, silently — a guard that rejects everything reports exactly as a guard that is never reached.
- **Never while a runner run is live on this work.** A live session is already waiting on this verdict, and a second comment would queue a second runner on the pull request with two sessions pushing to one branch. "This work" is a run named after the PR's issue or the PR itself (`run-liveness.cjs`); with several sessions live, "any runner run" would have declined forever and handed nothing back. The check covers the whole runner job, so a run in its rescue or recovery steps still counts. `agentic-watchdog.yml` sweeps open pipeline PRs with a red CI and dispatches this workflow again, so a verdict that landed while the runner was busy is picked up on the next sweep rather than by a human. The sweep re-raises the event; every decision stays in the fail-safe, made once, on current state. This is also the ordinary path for a run that read its red, spent the one fix round `agentic-pipeline-finalization` allows, read red again and ended: the verdict landed while it was live, so the sweep is what hands that PR to a fresh session.
- **Never a draft.** A draft has already said a channel stayed red, and its issue is already released.
- **Never a pull request labelled `ci-fix-hold`.** The live-session check above sees the two runner workflows and nothing else, so a session driven from the web app, the desktop app, or a human at a terminal is invisible to it — and a handback then wakes a second worker onto a branch somebody is already fixing. "Is a human working on this" is not observable from the Actions API, so it is **declared rather than detected**: put `ci-fix-hold` on the pull request to take the red CI yourself, remove it to hand it back. It is deliberately an opt-out and not a detector; nothing infers it, and nothing removes it for you.
- **Once per CI run, identified by its run id — once per head and base tip for a conflict.** The head SHA and the CI run id are written into the comment's marker, and the `workflow_run` path answers a run id once: the same event redelivered carries the same id, and answering twice would queue a second session. **This is deliberately not a cooldown.** A duration long enough for today's CI is a stall once a shard count grows, and one short enough for tomorrow double-asks today; event identity does not drift. What re-opens a run id is a *dispatch* — the watchdog's re-raise, or a human's — which bypasses the dedup, because a handback whose session died before pushing leaves the head and the run id unchanged and must not be skipped forever. Every ask counts against the limit, so the retry is bounded by the brake rather than by a guessed interval.
- **Bounded by `AGENTIC_CI_FIX_ATTEMPT_LIMIT`**, shared by red channels and conflicts. When it is spent the workflow converts the PR to a draft — which takes it out of the gate's selection before the unmarked-PR check can see it — labels the issue `blocked` with the PAT, and drops `in-progress`. That is the same terminal shape every other failure ends in, so `handle-failure.yml` chains the queue past it. A CI failure that is not converging must not become a new way to stall.

**A red check is not always CI's, and none of the three may assume it is.** PR #773 ended with `ci.yml` green on every job and the pull request still `unstable`: `agentic-closing-keyword-guard.yml` (#765) had failed on the PR title. Each reader missed it for its own reason, and each reason was the same shape — a scope narrowed to a name.

- `[await-ci]` filtered the machinery out of its verdict by a `^agentic-` **prefix**, so the guard exempted itself from the channels by being called `agentic-closing-keyword-guard.yml`. The session waited the full fourteen minutes, read GREEN, and ended having done exactly what it was told. That filter is now a **named list**, and anything not on it is a channel: a new check counts with no edit anywhere, and forgetting to declare new machinery costs a wait rather than a silent pass.
- The fail-safe fires on `workflow_run` for `"CI"` and, on dispatch, used to look up `ci.yml` by path — so a failure from any other workflow raised no event and, once asked, found nothing to hand back. It now evaluates every channel on the head.
- `agentic-auto-merge` was the one reader that got it right: it reads every run, refused to merge, and said so by failing its own job — which is announced to nobody. The gate now dispatches the fail-safe for every marked PR that is red or conflicting.

The generalisation is the rule already stated above, applied to workflow names: **fail closed**. A reader that decides what counts by matching a name pattern grants an exemption to every file that happens to match it, including files that do not exist yet.

**Nothing in either mechanism waits on a duration**, the same property the merge gate holds. `[await-ci]` ends when the runs end, bounded by the runner's own `timeout-minutes` — and reaching *that* is safe rather than silent, because a killed job leaves no live runner run and the fail-safe picks the PR up. The fail-safe's own dedup is event identity, and its brake counts attempts. The only intervals anywhere are poll cadences — the watchdog's cron, the script's `--interval-seconds` — and no decision reads them.

The handback lands as an `issue_comment` on a pull request, where `agentic-prompt` resolves `entity` to `pr <n>` and leaves `issue` empty — so the runner's `agentic-run-state` and `agentic-rescue` steps skip. That is right rather than unfortunate: the branch is already pushed and the PR already exists, so there is nothing to rescue, and the gate wakes on the push's CI and on the session ending. What the session owes is a green CI on a branch that already exists — `agentic-pipeline-ci-fix`.

**A conflict with the base is handed back the same way.** The gate merges only a head that contains the base's tip, and with several sessions live the base moves under every open PR. A PR that conflicts with it can neither be brought up to date nor merged, and before the gate nothing handed it to anyone. The fail-safe asks about it only on a dispatch — the gate's, or a re-raise — and only on GitHub's own `dirty`, read fresh rather than trusted from whoever dispatched; the `workflow_run` path answers a CI run and nothing else. The handback names the base tip the head conflicts with and tells the session to merge `origin/main` in, resolve, re-verify, push and wait for CI — the conflict variant of `agentic-pipeline-ci-fix`.

## Shared composite actions

They live in `.github/actions/`: `agentic-prompt` builds the trigger context both runners hand to their agent, `agentic-assign` picks and assigns the next issue — reading its rules from `.github/scripts/assignability.cjs` and its GitHub reads from `.github/scripts/issue-api.cjs`, which is why every workflow that assigns must check the repository out first — `agentic-run-state` reports whether a finished session left its issue terminal and whether the remaining job budget can carry another attempt, `agentic-rescue` salvages a feature branch from a run that ended before opening its PR and settles the issue either way, `agentic-recover-blocked` releases an issue whose assignment was dropped, and `agentic-auto-merge` is the merge gate — it merges a marked PR only when it is green on top of its base, whatever account opened it, releasing any workflow run parked as `action_required` on the way.
